introduction: “In the divine verses both fellowship with all peoples and avoidance of the people of hypocrisy and corruption have been revealed.” This guide holds the two together. It opens with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá visiting Christian friends at Christmas and with kindness even to enemies; it turns to the plain observation that “association is contagious” and that the company one keeps forms the soul; and it ends with a long series of commands to keep away from those who work against the Faith, and with a table talk that distinguishes harm to oneself from harm to others. Every tradition has both halves. Proverbs warns that “a companion of fools shall be destroyed”, Paul that “evil communications corrupt good manners”, Confucius to “have no friends not equal to yourself”, and the Dhammapada, which the guide itself quotes, to walk alone rather than with a fool. Against these stand Jesus, “a friend of publicans and sinners”, who said the sick need the physician, and the householder who would not have the tares pulled up. Paul’s letters show a community trying, as these readings do, to draw the line.
questions: Paul says he never meant believers to avoid the immoral “of this world”, only those within the community. Where do the readings draw their line: at belief, at conduct, or at intent?
“They that be whole need not a physician.” Reading 24 observes that some who went to help were themselves changed. What decides whether one goes as physician or stays away?
“Count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.” How do the readings keep avoidance from becoming hostility?
The householder forbids pulling up the tares “lest ye root up also the wheat”. What risk in the readings’ commands to shun does the parable name?
Confucius and the Dhammapada advise friendship only with equals or betters. If everyone followed that, who would befriend the one who needs a better friend?

outside.why: Among the heedless, the friends should become the cause of awareness. Ye are the light of the world; let your light so shine before men.
The image for influence that works by mixing: the kingdom is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
“The people of God must associate.” Asked why he ate with publicans and sinners, Jesus answered: they that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
Love and kindness even to enemies. Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, that ye may be the children of your Father, who sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
“Let no sweetness of tongue beguile you; consider the motive of every soul.” Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
Both halves of the reading in one sentence: I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Religion must not become a cause of hatred. The Qur’an: Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them.

Both fellowship with all and avoidance of the corrupt have been revealed. Paul draws the same double line: not to keep company with the immoral who are called brothers, yet not to shun the immoral of this world, for then must ye needs go out of the world.
A Christmas visit to Christian friends. At the well a woman is astonished to be asked for water: for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.

“Treasure the companionship of the righteous and eschew all fellowship with the ungodly.” The Psalter opens with it: blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
He should treasure the company of those who have renounced the world. He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
There are persons whose words are life-imparting. Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend by hearty counsel.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
The company of the ungodly increaseth sorrow. Paul quotes a Greek poet for it: be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
“Association is contagious.” Confucius’s rule is blunt: have no friends not equal to yourself.
Avoid the unworthy, or morals are corrupted. Make no friendship with an angry man, lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.
In the garden of the heart plant only flowers of love. Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.

Grace conditional on the fellowship of one or two holy souls. Emerson says where such a friend is to be had: the only way to have a friend is to be one. What does choosing good company ask of the chooser?
“Trust no man save him whose breast hath been dilated by God.” Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
With a dangerous soul, keep only a formal acquaintance. Paul’s version of distance without enmity: have no company with him; yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

“Consort with all religions” does not apply to a thief or a philanderer. Jesus was reproached for exactly such company: a gluttonous man and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. He went as a physician. When is that the right model, and when is the reading’s caution?
After three gatherings with no effect, withdraw. Whosoever shall not receive you, nor hear your words, when ye depart, shake off the dust of your feet.
Some who went among the corrupt to help them were themselves changed. Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
People whose breath extinguishes devotion. Ye did run well; who did hinder you? A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.

One may pass through foul air unharmed, but living in it is another matter. Aristotle distinguishes degrees too: one cannot be a friend to many people in the perfect sense. Do the readings’ cautions concern acquaintance, or intimacy?

Evil companions turn the good bad. The Dhammapada adds a distinction among the foolish: the fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least so far; the fool who thinks himself wise is a fool indeed. Which of the two is dangerous company?
Who would advise you to hug a serpent? Proverbs on a pleasant danger: at the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
Hold aloof from the sowers of sedition. Mark them which cause divisions and offences, and avoid them.
“The words of Christ” and the letters after him are cited for staying with the firm. The hardest of them: receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed.
Beware of meeting souls whose only purpose is sedition. A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject.
Associate not with those from whom you perceive hypocrisy. The Qur’an on hypocrites: their figures please thee, and if they speak thou givest ear; they are the enemy, so beware of them.
Draw not near to hearts veiled from the mention of God. When ye hear the revelations of Allah rejected and derided, sit not with them until they engage in some other conversation.
“Take not the unbelievers as friends in place of the believers”: the language is the Qur’an’s, and Paul’s too: be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers.
When ye find those who have turned away, avoid them. The servants of the Beneficent walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish address them answer: Peace.

“Consort not with Mine enemies.” In the parable the servants offer to pull up the tares, and the householder forbids it: lest ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest. Who is able to tell, now, which is which?
Some evils harm only the doer, and kindness to such is owed. He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
The reading is this verse, quoted: if a traveller does not meet with one who is his better, or his equal, let him firmly keep to his solitary journey; there is no companionship with a fool.

shortfall: Readings 36 to 56 are some twenty short commands, in nearly the same words, to shun enemies of the Faith and those who have turned away; a handful of scriptural parallels answer all of them, and the remaining readings were not each given one.
